title: One Sun, Two Earths: How Ice Can Lock a Planet in the Cold
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Entropy production and multiple equilibria: the case of the ice-albedo feedback
source.authors: C. Herbert, D. Paillard, and B. Dubrulle

intro.summary: This lesson draws on four sources: two encyclopedia articles (on the ice–albedo feedback and on Snowball Earth) and two research papers. The core paper (Herbert, Paillard and Dubrulle, 2011) uses a very simple whole-planet energy-balance model. It shows that when ice makes the planet more reflective, the same sunlight can support three climate states: a frozen 'snowball', a warm ice-free state, and an unstable state in between. Because the two stable states overlap over a range of sunlight, the climate depends on its history (hysteresis). A second paper (von Paris et al., 2013) finds that a thick CO2 atmosphere, or the reddish light of M-dwarf stars, can largely mask the feedback. The main limitation is that both papers use highly idealised models: a single average temperature, or prescribed atmospheres with no clouds. Their exact thresholds are illustrative, not predictions for the real Earth. Whether ancient Earth ever froze completely is still debated. The lesson does not cover the core paper's main technical novelty, a 'maximum entropy production' principle for picking out climate states, nor the detailed modern Arctic and Antarctic estimates. Those make good follow-up topics, along with bifurcation theory, the carbonate–silicate thermostat and snowball deglaciation.
background: Albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight a surface reflects: fresh snow reflects most of it, open ocean very little.
A planet's average temperature settles where the energy it absorbs from its star equals the heat it radiates back to space.
A feedback is a loop in which a change causes effects that push the original change further (positive) or back (negative).
Rocks deposited by glaciers can sometimes be dated and placed on an ancient map, which is how geologists found hints of ice near the ancient equator.
intro.aha: Under exactly the same sunlight, a planet can sit stably either frozen solid or comfortably warm, and once frozen it stays frozen until it is pushed far past the point where it fell in.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Ice is bright. When a planet cools and ice spreads, the planet reflects more sunlight and so cools further; when it warms and ice melts, it absorbs more and warms further. In 1969 Budyko and Sellers asked how far this loop can go. Could it tip a whole planet into a frozen state, and could that frozen state then stay put?
primer.quote: Because ice is very reflective, it reflects far more solar energy back to space than open water or any other land cover.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: Herbert and colleagues built a stripped-down model of Earth with one surface temperature and one air temperature, linked by sunlight, infrared radiation and a surface heat flux. They let the planet's reflectivity rise smoothly as the surface cools below freezing. Then they asked, for each strength of sunlight, which temperatures are balanced and which of those balances survive a small nudge. A separate study by von Paris and colleagues computed how reflective icy planets look from space under different stars and atmospheres.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: With a fixed albedo the model has just one balanced climate, near today's. With ice–albedo feedback switched on, a band of sunlight levels (about 0.98 to 1.08 times today's, in this model) allows three balanced climates at once. At today's sunlight these are a snowball near 249 K (about −24 °C), a warm state near 287 K (about 14 °C), and an unstable one near 275 K between them. The two outer states are stable; the middle one is a knife-edge.
primer.quote: the temperature and the ice cover of the planet are linked in a positive feedback which gives birth to multiple equilibria for some values of the solar constant: fully ice-covered Earth, ice-free Earth and an intermediate unstable solution.

primer.heading: Memory in the climate
primer.body: Because two stable climates overlap, the climate you end up in depends on where you started. A planet that falls into the snowball stays frozen even after sunlight returns to the level at which it froze. To escape, it must be pushed past a second, higher tipping point. Climate scientists call this path-dependence hysteresis.
primer.quote: Thus the hysteresis curve obtained for the temperature stems from the bifurcation structure of the dynamical system as two back-to-back saddle-node bifurcations.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and the limits
primer.body: This mechanism is a leading explanation for 'Snowball Earth' episodes about 717–635 million years ago, and for why escaping them may have needed huge volcanic CO2 build-ups. It also shapes today's Arctic warming. Yet the evidence that Earth froze completely is contested, and some scientists favour a 'slushball' with open tropical water. Von Paris and colleagues show that the feedback can be much weaker under thick CO2 atmospheres or around red-dwarf stars. All of these models are heavily simplified.
primer.quote: For planets around M stars, the ice-albedo feedback is almost entirely masked at high CO2 pressures (albedo change less than 0.04).

concepts.title: Sunlight in, heat out: where a planet settles
concepts.idea: A planet warms or cools until the heat it radiates equals the sunlight it absorbs, so a more reflective planet settles at a colder temperature.

predict.question: A planet sits settled and steady. Then its whole surface turns brighter, because fresh snow covers dark rock. The Sun does not change. If the surface then stays this bright, what happens to the planet's temperature over the following years?
options: It cools, then levels off at a new, colder settled temperature
It keeps cooling forever, because it now absorbs less than it loses
It stays the same, because the sunlight arriving hasn't changed
It warms, because the snow traps heat at the surface
why: Correct. A brighter surface keeps less sunlight, so the planet loses more heat than it gains and cools. Cooling makes it glow less, so the gap closes at a new, colder crossing where the two match again.
It does keep less at first, but as it cools it also glows less. The loss shrinks until it equals the smaller intake, so the cooling stops.
What counts is the sunlight the planet keeps, not the sunlight that arrives. A brighter surface bounces more of the same sunlight back to space, so it keeps less.
Snow can insulate the ground locally. In this balance, though, its key effect is reflecting sunlight, which means less heat in and a colder settled temperature.

terms.means: The share of incoming sunlight a planet reflects straight back to space: 0 is perfectly black, 1 is a perfect mirror
Sunlight absorbed minus heat radiated away. Positive means the planet warms, negative means it cools
The temperature where absorbed sunlight exactly equals heat radiated, so net heating is zero and the planet stops changing

model.title: Sunlight kept versus heat glowed away, at every temperature
model.note: Teaching model: a one-layer planet. It keeps ¼ × sunlight × (1 − reflectiveness) and radiates σT⁴ times a fixed factor of 0.61. That factor stands in for the whole greenhouse effect and is tuned so that reflectiveness 0.3 with today's Sun gives about 288 K. There are no oceans, clouds or separate air layers, and reflectiveness stays fixed instead of changing with temperature. Numbers are illustrative, not the papers' results.

outputs.label: Heat gained minus heat lost, right now

steps.say: The flat dashed line is the sunlight arriving on each square metre of this planet. It doesn't depend on how warm the planet is.
The solid flat line is the part the planet keeps. The rest bounces back to space. This slider sets how much bounces.
The rising curve is the heat the planet glows away into space. A hotter planet glows much, much more.
This slider sets the Sun's strength compared with today's. Both flat lines move with it.
And this marker is the planet's temperature right now. Let's see where it wants to go.

explore.prompt: You've seen a planet slide to the crossing. Now build planets to order: change how reflective they are, how strong their Sun is, and where they start.

goals.text: Under today's Sun, make a planet that settles colder than the freezing point of water
hints: Which slider changes how much of the same sunlight the planet keeps?
Push reflectiveness up and watch the 'Settles here' marker slide left toward the freezing line.
Somewhere between 0.4 and 0.5 the settled temperature drops past 273 K.

goals.text: Make a planet that is still heating up even though it is already hotter than 300 K
hints: A planet heats up only while it keeps more sunlight than it glows away. Where is it on the picture when that happens?
Put the current temperature just above 300 K. Then move the crossing so it sits to the right of that marker.
Make the planet darker, or the Sun stronger, until 'Settles at' is a few degrees above your current temperature.

feedback.correct: Right. Brightening cuts the sunlight kept, so the planet runs a deficit and cools. Cooling shrinks its glow until out matches in again at a lower crossing. It levels off; it doesn't fall forever.
feedback.incorrect: The key is the balance. What matters is sunlight kept, not sunlight arriving, and the heat lost falls steeply as the planet cools. So a brighter planet cools until its smaller glow matches its smaller intake, then stops at a colder settled temperature.

steps.say: Start a planet cold, at 220 K, under today's Sun with 30% of sunlight bounced back. At this temperature it keeps far more sunlight than it glows away.
That difference, sunlight kept minus heat lost, is the net heating. It's positive here, so the planet warms. As it warms, it glows more, and the gap narrows.
Near 288 K the glowing curve meets the flat line. Net heating is close to zero, so the planet stops changing. This crossing is the equilibrium temperature.
Now overshoot to 320 K. The planet glows away more than it keeps, so net heating turns negative and it cools back toward the same crossing. From either side, it slides to where in equals out.
Now make the planet more reflective. The share of sunlight bounced back is called albedo. Raise it from 0.3 to 0.6: the kept-sunlight line drops, so the crossing must slide left.
The same Sun now gives a planet that settles near 251 K, about −22 °C, well below freezing. Only the brightness changed.
Same sunlight, brighter surface, colder planet. That one lever, how much light bounces away, is what ice controls on a real planet.

understand.explanation: Every planet takes in sunlight and glows heat back out to space, and the glow grows steeply with temperature. If it keeps more than it glows away, it warms. If it glows more than it keeps, it cools. Either way it slides to the one temperature where the two match. Raising albedo, the share of sunlight bounced straight back, lowers what the planet keeps, so that crossing sits at a colder temperature. Herbert and colleagues (s3) built a simple energy-balance model with separate ground and air layers. With albedo fixed at 0.15, it has exactly one balanced temperature, near 288 K, about today's global mean. Real planets are messier: greenhouse gases, clouds and oceans all shift the numbers, and our model lumps all of that into one fixed factor.
understand.quote: This low temperature was maintained by the high albedo of the ice sheets, which reflected most incoming solar energy into space.
understand.quote_where: Snowball Earth article, section 'During the frozen period'

connect.caption: The teaching model's rule. Left, sunlight kept: S is the Sun's strength (Sunlight slider), α the albedo (Reflectiveness), and ξ = 0.25 spreads sunlight over a spinning sphere, as in s3's Table 1. Right, heat glowed away: σ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant; ε = 0.61 stands in for the greenhouse effect. T (Settles at) makes both sides equal. s3's two-layer model has the same ingredients split between ground and air.

concepts.recap: A planet settles where the sunlight it keeps equals the heat it glows away, so the more sunlight it reflects, the colder that settling point.

concepts.title: Cold makes ice, ice makes cold
concepts.idea: Colder temperatures mean more ice, more ice means higher albedo, and higher albedo means less absorbed sunlight and more cooling, so the loop amplifies a change in either direction.

predict.question: Keep both links strong, but flip the starting push to a 1-degree warming instead of a cooling. What does the loop do?
options: Amplifies it: the planet ends up warmer than the push alone would make it
Damps it: the loop only amplifies cooling, so the warming fades away
Turns it around: the warming ends up as a cooling
Nothing: the loop needs new ice to form, so warming leaves it idle
why: Right. Warming shrinks the ice and exposes darker ground or water. The planet reflects less and absorbs more sunlight, which adds more warming. The same links run in reverse.
Tempting, because the story is usually told with ice forming. But every link works both ways: less ice means less reflection, just as more ice means more.
A sign flip would need an odd number of 'opposite-direction' links. This loop has two (warmer→less ice, brighter→less absorbed), and they cancel, so the change keeps its direction.
Melting ice is just as much a change in ice cover as forming ice. Losing bright ice drives the loop as surely as gaining it.

terms.means: The share of incoming sunlight that a surface or a whole planet reflects back to space
A loop in which a change sets off effects that push it further in the same direction
The share of a change that comes back around the loop as extra change on each trip

model.title: A small temperature push travelling round the ice loop
model.note: Teaching model: the loop is cut down to two adjustable links: how much ice cover changes per degree, and how much brighter the planet gets per unit of ice. The last two links (brighter means less sunlight absorbed, and less absorbed means colder) are fixed at full strength. The change is added up over 8 trips round the loop. There is no limit from ice running out or covering everything, and no seasons, clouds or atmosphere. Node numbers are changes in the model's own units. All numbers are illustrative, not the papers' data.

controls.label: How strongly temperature changes the ice
How much brighter extra ice makes the planet

outputs.label: Share of a change that comes back each trip
How many times bigger the change ends up
outputs.expr: 1 + gain + gain^2 + gain^3 + gain^4 + gain^5 + gain^6 + gain^7 + gain^8

steps.say: Four boxes in a ring: the planet's temperature, its ice cover, the sunlight it reflects, and the sunlight it absorbs. Each arrow shows what pushes what.
This slider gives the planet a small starting push. Right now it is a cooling of one degree.
This slider sets how strongly a change in temperature grows or shrinks the ice.
This one sets how much brighter the planet gets when the ice spreads.
Keep an eye on this box. It shows the final temperature change once the push has gone round the ring.

explore.prompt: Play with the two links. Find out what it takes for the ring to turn a small push into a big change, and what it takes to make the ring do nothing.

goals.text: Keep the starting push at a 1-degree cooling, and make the loop turn it into 3 degrees of cooling or more
hints: The ring only returns a lot if every link passes the change along strongly.
Raising just one slider leaves the other link as a bottleneck. Watch the 'comes back each trip' box as you move both.
Well over half of each change has to come back on every trip, and that needs both links near the top.

goals.text: Keep the ice very sensitive to temperature, yet stop the loop from amplifying the push at all
hints: A loop is a chain. What happens if one link passes nothing on?
Ask what extra ice would do to the temperature if it were no brighter than the ground it covers.
Leave the ice slider high and work on the brightness link instead.

feedback.correct: Yes. The loop has no preferred direction. Warming melts bright ice, the darker surface absorbs more sunlight, and that adds more warming. The model gives the same amplification for a warming push as for a cooling one.
feedback.incorrect: You may have pictured the loop as something that only builds ice. Every link works both ways. Less ice means less reflection, more absorbed sunlight and more warming. Two 'opposite-direction' links cancel, so a warming stays a warming and grows.

steps.say: Start with ice that ignores temperature entirely. The one-degree cooling stays exactly one degree, because nothing comes back around the ring.
Now let cooling grow the ice. Ice is bright, so the planet reflects a larger share of sunlight. That share is its albedo, and it rises.
A higher albedo means less sunlight absorbed. As you saw before, a planet that absorbs less settles colder. So the cooling grows.

Follow the signs round. Cooler means more ice: a flip. More ice means brighter. Brighter means less absorbed: another flip. Less absorbed means cooler. Two flips cancel, so the change keeps its direction. That is a positive feedback.
Each trip round, a share of the change comes back as extra change. That share is the loop gain, here 25%. One degree becomes 1 + 0.25 + 0.06 + … ≈ 1.33 degrees.
The gain is the links multiplied together, so both have to be strong. Raise them both and the same one-degree push now ends up near 2.7 degrees of cooling.
A small push, a large result, and no new cause was added: the ring is feeding on its own output. In real climate models this growth stops only when the ice runs out or covers everything.

understand.explanation: Each link in the loop passes a change along. Cooling grows ice; ice is bright, so the planet's albedo rises; it absorbs less sunlight; and a planet that absorbs less settles colder. The two 'opposite-direction' links cancel, so the loop pushes the change further the same way. The same logic runs in reverse for warming: less ice, a darker surface, more absorbed sunlight, more warming. Budyko and Sellers built this link into simple energy-balance climate models in 1969 and found it could act as a powerful feedback. Herbert and colleagues encode it by making albedo rise smoothly as surface temperature falls. Today the loop runs in the warming direction: shrinking Arctic sea ice is one of the main reasons the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average since 1979. The model's link strengths are made up. Real strengths depend on season, sunlight, clouds and the air, so the true amplification has to be estimated with full climate models.
understand.quote: However, if warming occurs, then higher temperatures would decrease ice-covered area, and expose more open water or land. The albedo decreases, and so more solar energy is absorbed, leading to more warming and greater loss of the reflective parts of the cryosphere. Inversely, cooler temperatures increase ice cover, which increases albedo and results in greater cooling, which makes further ice formation more likely.

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule, not an equation from the papers. The push (blue) returns a share g on every trip round the loop. g is the ice link a multiplied by the brightness link b, so a weak link anywhere keeps g small. The papers build the same link into the climate itself: Herbert et al. make albedo a smooth function of surface temperature (their Eq. 18), so cooling raises albedo.

concepts.recap: Cold grows bright ice, bright ice reflects sunlight away, and less sunlight means more cold. Run backwards, the same loop turns warming into more warming.

concepts.title: One Sun, three possible climates
concepts.idea: When albedo rises as the planet cools, the absorbed-sunlight curve bends into an S-shape that can cross the emitted-heat curve three times, giving three balanced temperatures for the same sunlight.

predict.question: Picture a planet whose ice is dirty and dark, so icy ground is only a little more reflective than ice-free ground. Its sunlight is set in the middle of the range where an Earth-like planet has three balances. How many balanced temperatures would you expect?
options: Still three: any ice at all creates the extra crossings
Just one: the kept-sunlight curve barely bends, so the steep heat curve crosses it once
Two: a frozen climate and a warm one, with nothing in between
None: with dark ice the planet can never balance
why: Tempting, because the feedback still exists. But three crossings need a deep S, with a big drop between the warm and icy shelves. A small gap leaves the curve almost flat, and the steep heat curve passes it once.

Right. The size of the jump in reflectiveness sets how deep the S bends. With dark ice the kept-sunlight curve is nearly a flat line, and a flat line meets the steadily rising heat curve exactly once.

Two crossings would need the heat curve to just touch the S, which happens only at one exact sunlight. A curve that starts above the heat curve when cold and ends below it when hot crosses it an odd number of times: one or three.
Somewhere the heat curve always overtakes the kept sunlight. Cold planets glow away almost nothing, and hot ones glow away a lot. So there is always at least one crossing.

terms.means: Several different temperatures at which heat in equals heat out, all under the same sunlight
Climate scientists' name for the strength of sunlight reaching the planet (the Sun slider)

model.title: Sunlight kept versus heat glowed away, now with ice that forms in the cold
model.note: Teaching model: the same one-layer planet as before (it keeps ¼ × sunlight × (1 − reflectiveness) and radiates 0.61σT⁴). It now uses the smooth ice switch of Herbert et al. (2011, Eq. 18). Reflectiveness slides from the slider's ice-free value up to 0.6 for fully icy ground, centred on 273.15 K (as in the paper) over a width of 10 K (the paper used 15 K). The paper used a two-layer model, so the icy value and width here were tuned until this one-layer toy shows three balances at today's Sun. They fall at about 251, 275 and 286 K, close to the paper's 249, 275 and 287 K but not its results. On the slider's 5% steps, the toy has three balances from 100% to 110% of today's sunlight; the paper's model found about 98–108%. The counter finds crossings by checking the curves every 5 K. If the ice-free reflectiveness is set at 0.6 or more, ice adds nothing. There are no oceans, clouds or heat transport. Numbers are illustrative.

outputs.label: Heat gained minus heat lost, right now

series.label: Sunlight kept
series.expr: 342 * sun / 100 * (1 - albedo - (ice_on > 0.5 ? max(0.6, albedo) - albedo : 0) * logistic(0.2 * (273.15 - x)))

steps.say: Same picture as before: the blue line is sunlight the planet keeps, the steep curve is heat glowing away, and the marker is the temperature right now. Where they cross, heat in equals heat out.
One new switch lets ice form when the planet is cold. Icy ground bounces back more sunlight, up to 0.6. With the switch on, the reflectiveness slider sets the ice-free ground.
This new counter shows how many temperatures balance heat in and heat out. Keep an eye on it.

explore.prompt: Keep the ice switched on and play with the Sun. Watch how the S-shaped kept-sunlight curve rises and sinks against the heat curve, and how the counter responds.

goals.text: With ice forming, find a Sun brighter than today's that still leaves the planet three balanced temperatures.
hints: Three crossings need the heat curve to thread through the steep middle of the S. Brightening lifts the whole S. How far can it rise before the cold end stops crossing?
Turn the ice on first, then brighten the Sun one step at a time while watching the counter and the cold shelf on the left.
The window of three closes within a few steps above today's sunlight, so don't jump far.

goals.text: Starting from today's Sun with ice on, dim the Sun and stop at the first setting where the warm climate has vanished and only one balance is left.
hints: Dimming lowers the whole S. Which crossing loses touch first, the frozen one or the warm one?
Watch the small bump of the blue curve between about 275 and 290 K. As the Sun dims it sinks toward the heat curve until it no longer pokes above it.
Move down one step at a time and stop the moment the counter drops. It happens very close to today's value.

feedback.correct: Yes. Three balances need a deep S. With dark ice the jump in reflectiveness is small, the kept-sunlight curve stays nearly flat, and the steadily rising heat curve crosses it only once.
feedback.incorrect: It is easy to think ice alone makes three climates. In fact the extra crossings come from how sharply the kept-sunlight curve bends. A small brightness gap gives a shallow bend, and the steep heat curve passes straight through it once.

steps.say: Start with ice switched off. Reflectiveness is fixed, so the kept-sunlight line is flat. The steep heat curve crosses it once, near 288 K, and the counter reads 1.
Now let ice form. Above about 290 K almost nothing changes. Below freezing the ground turns icy, reflectiveness climbs toward 0.6, and the kept-sunlight line drops to a lower shelf.

Around freezing the line climbs steeply into an S: low when cold, high when warm. The heat curve crosses it three times; the counter reads 3. Several balances under one Sun are called multiple equilibria.
Slide the marker to 250 K, near the cold crossing. This is a frozen planet whose icy brightness keeps it cold. Heat gained minus heat lost is close to zero.
At 275 K the marker sits on the in-between crossing, on the steep part of the S, and the net is again about zero. The third crossing, the warm one, is near 286 K, close to today's Earth.
Now change the Sun's strength, which scientists call the solar constant. Dim it to 90%. The whole S sinks, and the middle and warm crossings vanish. Only the frozen one is left.
Brighten it to 120%. Now the cold shelf rises above the heat curve, the frozen crossing disappears, and only the warm climate is left.
Back to today's Sun: three crossings again. Three climates exist only inside a window of sunlight. Inside that window, the sunlight alone does not tell you which one the planet has.

understand.explanation: When reflectiveness depends on temperature, the kept-sunlight curve stops being flat. It sits on a low shelf when the planet is icy, a high shelf when it is ice-free, and climbs steeply around freezing. The heat glowed away rises smoothly and steeply, so it can thread through that S and cross it three times: a frozen balance, an in-between one and a warm one, all under the same Sun. Herbert, Paillard and Dubrulle (2011) showed this with an idealised two-layer energy-balance model and a smooth ice switch. At today's sunlight they found balances near 249 K (a snowball), 275 K and 287 K, and three balances only for sunlight between about 98% and 108% of today's; outside that window one remains. The exact edges depend on model details (the toy here gives roughly 100–110%), and neither model has oceans, clouds or heat moving between latitudes. Earlier simple models by Budyko and Sellers (1969) had already found the same frozen and present-day pair.
understand.quote: for certain values of the solar constant, three solutions coexist. This range can be determined to be approximately 0.98 S0 ≤ S ≤ 1.08 S0. Outside this range, only one solution subsists.

connect.caption: This is the paper's Eq. 18, the ice switch behind the S. α_{F} is the ice-free reflectiveness (the reflectiveness slider). α_{I} is the fully icy value, 0.6 in this toy, and the gap α_{I} − α_{F} is the 'extra reflectiveness of icy ground' output. T_{g} is the surface temperature (the marker), and T_{0} = 273.15 K is where the switch is centred. ΔT sets how gradual it is: 10 K here, 15 K in the paper. Multiply sunlight by (1 − α) and you get the bent blue curve.

concepts.recap: Ice that brightens a cooling planet bends the kept-sunlight curve into an S. In a window of sunlight it crosses the heat curve three times; outside it, one climate remains.

concepts.title: Two valleys and a hilltop
concepts.idea: At each balance point, a small temperature nudge is either pushed back (the snowball and warm states are stable) or pushed further away (the middle state is an unstable tipping point).

predict.question: Real planets are jostled all the time by weather, eruptions and slow orbital wobbles. In this model at today's sunlight, with ice forming, where would you expect to find a planet after a very long time?
options: In the warm state or the snowball, but practically never on the middle balance
Equally likely at any of the three balances
On the middle balance, because it is a compromise between the extremes
Always in the warm state, because today's Earth is warm
why: Right: jostling only shakes a planet around inside a valley, so it stays near the snowball or the warm state. The first jolt knocks it off the hilltop, and it rolls into one of the valleys.
Tempting, because all three are true balance points. But a balance only lasts if nudges die out, and at the middle one every nudge grows.
Being 'in between' sounds safe, but the middle crossing is the hilltop: the slightest push sends the planet off toward one extreme.
The warm state is a valley, but so is the snowball. Which one a planet ends in depends on where it started, not on which is 'normal'.

terms.means: A balance point the planet returns to after a small nudge, like a ball in a valley
A balance point that any small nudge pushes the planet away from, like a ball on a hilltop
A threshold where a small change sends a system off to a very different state

model.title: Sunlight kept versus heat glowed away, and where the planet drifts from any start
model.note: Teaching model: the same one-layer planet as before. It keeps ¼ × sunlight × (1 − reflectiveness) and radiates 0.61σT⁴, with the smooth ice switch of Herbert et al. (2011, Eq. 18). Reflectiveness rises from the slider's ice-free value to 0.6 for icy ground, centred on 273.15 K over a width of 10 K (the paper used 15 K). At today's sunlight with ice on, the balances fall near 251, 275 and 286 K. The paper's two-layer model gave 249, 275 and 287 K, so these are close but not its results. New here: the 'drift' readouts repeat a simple numerical settling rule eight times. Each round moves the temperature by (heat gained − heat lost) divided by how fast glowing grows with temperature, capped at 15 K a round. This is a shortcut for finding where the planet ends up, not the paper's time evolution, and it says nothing about how many years the trip takes. Very close to the middle crossing the planet leaves slowly, so eight rounds may not finish the trip. There are no oceans, clouds, seasons or heat transport. Numbers are illustrative.

outputs.label: Heat gained minus heat lost, right now
outputs.expr: 3.42 * sun * (1 - albedo - d_ice * logistic(0.2 * (273.15 - temp_now))) - 3.4587 * pow(temp_now / 100, 4)

series.label: Sunlight kept
series.expr: 342 * sun / 100 * (1 - albedo - (ice_on > 0.5 ? max(0.6, albedo) - albedo : 0) * logistic(0.2 * (273.15 - x)))

steps.say: Same picture as last time, with ice switched on: the sunlight-kept curve bends, and it crosses the heat-glowed curve three times.
New: this second line shows where the planet drifts to if you start it at the marked temperature and then leave it alone.
Slide the starting temperature, and the drift line jumps to wherever the planet ends up. The rounds in between trace the trip.

explore.prompt: Keep today's sunlight and the ice switched on. Play with starting temperatures near the freezing line and watch where the drift line lands.

goals.text: Keep today's sunlight with ice forming. Start the planet within 5 K of the freezing line, yet have it end up in the deep freeze.
hints: The freezing line and the middle crossing are not quite the same place.
At each start you try, check the heat-gained-minus-lost readout: a negative number means the planet is cooling.
Only one of the starts allowed here sits on the cold side of the middle crossing.

goals.text: Same sunlight and reflectiveness, still starting within 10 K of freezing: now make the planet end up in the warm climate.
hints: To end up warm, the start has to be on the warm side of the hilltop.
The middle crossing sits a little above freezing, so starting just above 0 °C may not be enough.
Step up through the starts above freezing one at a time, and stop at the first one where heat gained beats heat lost.

feedback.correct: Yes. Constant jostling keeps a planet rattling around inside a valley, near the snowball or the warm state. But the very first jolt knocks it off the middle balance, so nothing stays there for long.
feedback.incorrect: Being a balance point is not enough to last. What matters is whether nudges die out (a valley) or grow (a hilltop). Only the snowball and warm states pull a jostled planet back.

steps.say: Ice on, today's Sun: three crossings, near 251, 275 and 286 K. Start at 250 K. The kept curve sits just above the glowed curve, so the planet gains heat and drifts up, but only to the first crossing.
Now start a little warmer, at 260 K. Here glowing beats keeping, so the readout goes negative and the planet cools back down to the same crossing.
Push it up and it falls back. Push it down and it climbs back. A crossing like this is a stable equilibrium, a valley the planet rolls back into. This one is the snowball.
The warm crossing behaves the same way. Start at 290 K: the planet loses more than it gains and settles back near 286 K. That is a second valley.
Start at 280 K, below the warm crossing. Heat gained wins, so the planet warms back up to the same place.
Now go just 10 K colder, to 270 K, on the other side of the middle crossing. Here the bright ice tips the balance: cooling wins, and the planet slides all the way down to the snowball.

Two starts only 10 K apart end about 35 K apart. Around the middle crossing, every nudge grows instead of fading. It is an unstable equilibrium, a hilltop, and it acts as the tipping point between the two climates.

understand.explanation: A crossing is a temperature where heat gained equals heat lost, but that alone does not tell you whether a planet can stay there. Nudge it and look at the gap. At the snowball and warm crossings, a slightly warmer planet loses more than it gains and a slightly colder one gains more, so nudges fade: these are stable equilibria, two valleys. At the middle crossing, melting ice makes kept sunlight rise faster than glowing as the planet warms, so any nudge grows: an unstable equilibrium, the tipping point between the climates. Herbert, Paillard and Dubrulle (2011) found exactly this in their simple two-layer model. The ice-free and snowball states were always stable when they existed, and the middle state was unstable; they read this from whether the heating curve crosses zero going down or going up. They confirmed it with an energy 'landscape' that has two minima and one maximum at today's sunlight. This is a deliberately idealised model with no oceans, seasons or clouds, so it shows the mechanism, not Earth's real thresholds.
understand.quote: The stability can also be read directly on Fig.4 for the 1D-reduced system: stable equilibria correspond to roots of the function with negative derivative

check.task: With ice forming, raise the sunlight. Then find a starting temperature below the freezing line from which the planet still ends up in the warm climate.
check.hint: What decides the fate is which side of the middle crossing you start on, not which side of 0 °C. Watch where the middle crossing moves as the Sun brightens.
check.misconception: That the freezing line itself is the tipping point, so any planet that starts below 0 °C must freeze over.

connect.caption: The model's one-layer version of the paper's Eq. 28 (c_{pg} dT_{g}/dt = R_{g} + γ_{g}). The right side is the 'heat gained minus heat lost' readout. S is the sunlight slider, α(T) is the reflectiveness (higher where ice forms) and T is the starting-temperature marker. A balance is stable where the right side goes from positive to negative as T rises (snowball, warm), and unstable where it goes from negative to positive (middle).

concepts.recap: Where kept sunlight drops below the heat glowed away as temperature rises, nudges die out (the snowball and warm valleys). Where it climbs above, nudges grow (the middle hilltop, a tipping point).

concepts.title: Starlight and air set how hard the feedback bites
concepts.idea: Ice only cools a planet if its extra brightness shows from space; red-dwarf light, which is mostly near-infrared where ice is dark, and a thick CO2 atmosphere both shrink the albedo gap between icy and ice-free planets.

terms.means: Light with colours just past red. Our eyes cannot see it, but it still carries a lot of a star's energy.
Air molecules bouncing light around, mostly visible light. Thick air sends part of the starlight back to space before it reaches the ground.
A small, cool star, which astronomers also call an M star. Most of its light is near-infrared rather than visible. The paper uses the red dwarf AD Leo.

model.title: How much brighter does ice make a planet?
model.note: Teaching model: two otherwise identical planets with pure CO2 air. One is fully iced over. The other has a dark surface that reflects 0.10 of the light, like the paper's low-albedo case. Brightness changes smoothly with the logarithm of CO2 pressure between the paper's thin (0.1 bar) and dense (30 bar) cases. There are no clouds, water vapour, methane or ozone. These reported values are anchored to von Paris et al. (2013): the gap shrinking from 0.35 to 0.05 around the Sun in dense air, a gap under 0.04 for the red dwarf in dense air, and icy-planet values near 0.45 (Sun) and 0.20 (red dwarf) at 1 bar. The red dwarf's thin-air gap and all in-between values are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Light from a small red star

steps.say: Two planets, same star, same air. This bar is a planet covered in ice. Its height is the share of starlight it bounces back to space.
This bar is the same planet with no ice: dark ground and sea.
The third bar is the difference: how much extra light the ice sends away. That extra is what drives the cooling loop.
This slider thickens the planet's CO₂ air, from a tenth of Earth's air pressure up to 30 times it. One bar is about Earth's air pressure.
This switch swaps the Sun-like star for a small red star. Watch the bars change.

explore.prompt: Play with the star and the air. Try to hide the ice's brightness from space.

goals.text: Keep the Sun-like star and shrink the extra reflection from ice below 0.1
hints: With the star fixed, only one thing is left to change.
Thin air lets the ice show clearly. Something must outshine the ice from above.
You need air many times thicker than Earth's, well into double digits of bar.

goals.text: Shrink the extra reflection from ice below 0.04, the level the paper calls almost entirely masked
hints: Around the Sun-like star, even the thickest air leaves a gap of about 0.05.
Change what kind of light reaches the planet as well.
Combine the red star with air far thicker than Earth's.

predict.question: Ozone absorbs mainly blue and violet light, below about 0.5 micrometres. The paper also added lots of ozone to the air of a planet around the red dwarf. What happens to the difference ice makes?
options: It barely changes
It shrinks a lot, just as it does around the Sun
It grows, because ozone makes ice look brighter
It flips, so ice warms the planet
why: Right. A gas can only hide the ice at colours the star actually sends. The red dwarf emits little blue and violet light, so ozone has almost nothing to absorb. The paper found its effect 'almost negligible' for AD Leo.

Around the Sun, ozone does shrink the gap strongly in dense CO2 air, because the Sun is bright in blue and violet. A red dwarf sends little light at those colours, so the same gas has little to work on.
Absorbing gases remove light before it can bounce back. They make the planet darker from space, not the ice brighter. They can only shrink the gap.
Absorption can make ice's extra brightness hard to see, but it cannot make ice darker than open ground. At worst the gap shrinks toward zero.

feedback.correct: Yes. What matters is how much light the star sends at the colours where a gas or the ice acts. The red dwarf sends little blue and violet light, so ozone barely touches its planet's ice gap.
feedback.incorrect: The gap only shrinks when something acts at colours the star actually emits. Ozone works on blue and violet light. Little of the red dwarf's light is there, so the paper found ozone's effect almost negligible for AD Leo, even though it was large for the Sun.

steps.say: Start with a Sun-like star and thin air. The icy planet reflects 0.45 of the light, the ice-free one only 0.10. That 0.35 difference is the fuel of the ice-albedo loop: more ice, much more light sent away.
Now thicken the air. Air molecules bounce visible light back to space by themselves. This is called Rayleigh scattering. The ice-free planet gets brighter even though its ground has not changed.

At 30 bar the air itself is a bright veil. From space the ice-free planet looks almost as bright as the icy one. The difference falls to 0.05, which matches the paper's figure. Ice adds little extra cooling now.

Back to thin air, but now with a red dwarf, a small cool star that astronomers call an M star. Most of its light is near-infrared, just past red. Ice is bright in visible light but fairly dark in near-infrared.
So the icy planet around the red dwarf reflects only about 0.20. Even in thin air, ice adds little: the star's light lands mostly where ice is dark.
Add thick CO₂ as well. CO₂ soaks up near-infrared light, dimming the icy planet, and the air's own bounce lifts the ice-free one a little.
At 30 bar the difference is about 0.03. Ice is nearly invisible from space, so the loop barely bites. The paper calls this 'almost entirely masked'.

understand.explanation: The ice-albedo loop only works because ice makes the whole planet look brighter from space. Von Paris and colleagues (2013) measured that brightening with a computer model of light passing through an atmosphere. They used measured colour-by-colour reflectance of Antarctic ice and snow, the light of the Sun and of the red dwarf AD Leo, and CO2 pressures from 0.1 to 30 bar. A red dwarf's light is mostly near-infrared, where ice is dark, so icy planets there reflected roughly half as much as around the Sun. Thick CO2 hides the surface: around the Sun the icy-minus-ice-free gap fell from 0.35 to 0.05, and around the red dwarf it dropped below 0.04; small amounts of water vapour and methane trimmed it further. These are brightness calculations with fixed temperatures and no clouds, not full climate runs. They show how strongly the feedback can act, not what any real planet does.
understand.quote: For dense CO2 atmospheres of the order of a few to tens of bar, atmospheric rather than surface properties begin to dominate the planetary radiation budget. At high CO2 pressures, the ice-albedo feedback is strongly reduced for planets around M stars.

connect.caption: The paper's Equation 1. A_p is the planet's overall brightness from space, shown by the bars (linked here to the icy planet). A_p,λ is how bright the planet is at each colour λ: ice is bright in visible light and dark in near-infrared, and thick CO2 changes this too. F_∗,λ is how much light the star sends at each colour, which is what the star switch changes. The overall brightness is a star-weighted average, so a star that shines mostly where ice is dark makes ice count for little.

concepts.recap: Ice cools a planet only as much as its extra brightness shows from space: red-dwarf light and thick CO2 air both hide it, weakening the feedback.

concepts.title: Did Earth really freeze over?
concepts.idea: Glacial rocks that appear to have formed near the ancient equator suggest a runaway freeze, but each line of evidence has rival explanations, so a full 'snowball' versus a 'slushball' with open tropical water remains debated.

terms.means: The ancient magnetic direction locked into a rock as it formed, used to estimate the latitude where it formed
A rock of alternating iron-rich and iron-poor layers that needs an ocean low in oxygen to form
A layer of limestone or dolomite that sits sharply on top of a glacial deposit
The idea that a band of open or thinly iced water stayed around the equator during the great glaciations

concepts.recap: Rocks hint that ice reached the ancient tropics, and the ice–albedo loop explains how it could spread, but every clue has a rival reading, so a full snowball versus a slushball is still open.

understand.explanation: Glaciers leave distinctive rocks, and palaeomagnetism, the magnetic direction locked into a rock as it formed, suggests that some of these rocks from roughly 700 million years ago formed near the ancient equator. Models suggest that once ice reaches within about 25–30° of the equator, the ice–albedo loop runs away, so ice in the tropics was read as a sign of a full 'snowball Earth'. Two more clues seemed to fit: the return of banded iron formation, a layered iron rock that needs an oxygen-poor ocean, and a cap carbonate, a limestone layer that sits sharply on top of the glacial rocks. But each clue has a rival explanation, and some rocks of the same age look as if they formed in open, moving water. That leaves a slushball Earth, in which a band of open or thinly iced water survived around the equator, as a live alternative. These encyclopedia sources report the arguments on both sides of the debate and do not settle it.
understand.quote: Several unanswered questions remain, including whether Earth was a full "snowball" or a "slushball" with a thin equatorial band of open (or seasonally open) water.

activities.prompt: Look at the case as a geologist would. Read each clue, then look for the catch.

stages.label: Clue 1: glacial rocks in the tropics
stages.text: When sediments settle, tiny magnetic minerals line up with Earth's magnetic field. Their tilt records the latitude where the rock formed, though not the longitude. This method is called palaeomagnetism. It places some glacial sediments within 10 degrees of the ancient equator. The catch: the ancient magnetic field may not have looked like today's, and hot water from later mountain-building can reset a rock's magnetic signal. Many 'glacial' features, such as dropstones, scratches and jumbled boulder beds, can also form without ice. Only one deposit, the Elatina deposit of Australia, is described as formed at low latitude beyond doubt.

stages.label: Clue 2: iron rocks come back
stages.text: A banded iron formation is a layered iron-rich rock that forms only when the ocean is low in oxygen. After about 1.8 billion years ago these rocks almost disappear. The only extensive later ones sit with these glacial deposits. Supporters of a full freeze say an ocean sealed under sea ice was cut off from the oxygen in the air. The catch: these deposits are rare. They could have formed in isolated inland seas, stagnant at depth like today's Black Sea. They are also found layered between glacial sediments, which is awkward if they mark the end of the freeze.

stages.label: Clue 3: a limestone cap
stages.text: On top of many of these glacial deposits there is a sharp switch to a cap carbonate, a layer of limestone or dolomite metres to tens of metres thick. The snowball reading: a carbon-dioxide-rich air after the freeze made acid rain, which wore down rock and washed calcium into the sea, where it settled as carbonate. The catch: a very acidic ocean should dissolve carbonates, not lay them down. Some caps seem too thick for a quick melt, and many clearly glacial sequences have no cap at all. A sudden release of methane has been proposed as another explanation, at least for one cap.

stages.label: Counter-clues: signs of open water
stages.text: Rocks from the snowball periods include ripples shaped by waves, debris carried far by floating ice, and signs of photosynthesis, all of which point to open water. Glacial beds up to 5,500 metres thick, split by thin non-glacial layers, suggest that ice melted and re-formed again and again. Chemical weathering seems to have risen and fallen in cycles. A climate model with a full moving ocean failed to grow sea ice all the way to the equator. Melting a global ice cover is calculated to need about 130,000 ppm of carbon dioxide, a level some researchers consider unreasonably large.

stages.label: Two pictures left standing
stages.text: In a full snowball, the ocean is frozen over almost everywhere. In a slushball Earth, a band of open or thin-ice water survives around the equator, so the water cycle keeps running. Both pictures need an ice–albedo runaway to push ice far toward the tropics. They disagree about how far it got.

activities.takeaway: Every clue for a full freeze has a rival reading, and some rocks point to open water. The evidence fits widespread glaciation, but it does not settle how complete the freeze was.

activities.title: Weigh the evidence
activities.prompt: Sort each finding by what it does to the case for a fully frozen Earth.

cards.text: Magnetic signals place some glacial sediments within 10° of the ancient equator
cards.feedback: This is the original clue. If ice reached sea level in the tropics, the runaway loop suggests ice everywhere. The accuracy of these reconstructions is still questioned.

cards.text: Banded iron rocks reappear only alongside these glacial deposits
cards.feedback: Supporters read this as an ocean sealed under ice and starved of oxygen. Opponents point out that inland seas could do the same.

cards.text: Thick limestone caps sit sharply on top of glacial deposits
cards.feedback: The snowball story explains them as carbonate formed after an acid-rain melt. Critics note that acidic oceans should dissolve carbonate, and that many glacial sequences have no cap.

cards.text: Wave-formed ripples and far-travelled ice-rafted debris appear in rocks of the same age
cards.feedback: Waves and drifting ice need open water. They could come from small 'oases', but models suggest large areas of ocean stayed ice-free.

cards.text: Chemical weathering rose and fell in cycles within one glacial succession
cards.feedback: Cycles of warm and cold look more like recent ice-age cycles than like a planet frozen solid for millions of years.

cards.text: A climate model with a full moving ocean failed to form sea ice to the equator
cards.feedback: Simple models can be made to freeze over completely. A more realistic ocean model did not, which makes a hard snowball harder to produce.

cards.text: Later hot water from mountain-building can reset a rock's magnetic signal
cards.feedback: This undercuts the main supporting clue. A 'tropical' magnetic reading might not be original.

cards.text: The fossil record shows no clear mass-extinction-style change in life
cards.feedback: A whole-Earth freeze should have reshaped life, and that change has not been seen. A rebuttal is that the fossil record is thin in many of these places.

hints: Ask of each card: does it need ice everywhere, or does it need open water or a doubtful measurement?
Cards about waves, warm-cold cycles and models that won't freeze all point the same way.
activities.takeaway: The supporting clues are real, but each has a counter-argument, and several independent findings point to open water.

activities.question: Why did glaciers near the ancient equator suggest that the whole planet froze, and not just that the tropics got icy?

options.text: Models suggest that once ice spreads to within about 25–30° of the equator, the ice–albedo loop runs away until ice covers everything
options.feedback: Right. The runaway loop from earlier concepts means tropical sea-level ice is hard to explain without global ice. That is the logic of the snowball idea.

options.text: Because the equator is normally the coldest part of the planet
options.feedback: No. The equator gets the most direct sunlight and is the warmest. That is why ice there is so surprising.

options.text: Because rocks worldwide were dated to exactly the same year
options.feedback: No. Rocks this old can rarely be dated better than to within about a million years, so proving that glaciers everywhere existed at the same time is very hard.

options.text: Because tropical glaciers can form only when the poles are ice-free
options.feedback: No. Nothing in the sources says this. The argument rests on the runaway ice–albedo feedback, not on ice-free poles.

activities.question: After weighing all the clues, which statement best matches what the sources report?

options.text: A full snowball is proven: tropical glaciers, iron rocks and limestone caps settle it
options.feedback: Too strong. Each of these clues has a published rival explanation, and some rocks of the same age show open water.

options.text: The snowball idea is disproven: the glaciers were only local mountain ice
options.feedback: Too strong the other way. Evidence of sea-level glaciation in the tropics is accumulating, and the 'local' explanations are themselves contested.

options.text: Severe glaciation is widely accepted, but whether the freeze was total or left open tropical water is still debated; the ice–albedo feedback matters in either case
options.feedback: Right. The sources say the presence of glaciers is not disputed, the full-snowball versus slushball question remains open, and the ice–albedo feedback is important for both pictures.

options.text: The ice–albedo feedback played no part, because the ice was caused by moving continents
options.feedback: No. Continent positions may have helped start the cooling, but both the snowball and slushball pictures rely on the ice–albedo loop to spread the ice.

concepts.title: Easy to freeze, hard to thaw
concepts.idea: Because the snowball and warm states coexist over a range of sunlight, a frozen planet stays frozen as sunlight recovers and only thaws once it is pushed past a second, higher tipping point, so the climate remembers its history.

predict.question: On a snowball Earth the Sun barely changed. Instead, volcanoes slowly added CO2, which warms a planet much like turning up the sunlight slider. Compare two amounts of warming: what would have stopped Earth freezing in the first place, and what was needed to escape the snowball. How do they compare?
options: About the same: escape just undoes the cooling that froze it
Far more: the push has to pass the second, higher tipping point
Less: once a little ice melts, the rest follows easily
None: a frozen planet thaws by itself if you wait long enough
why: This is tempting if the climate simply retraced its path. But the bright ice keeps a frozen planet cold until the upper tipping point, so undoing the original cooling is not enough.

Right. The snowball valley survives well above the freezing threshold, so greenhouse gas had to pile up far beyond it. One estimate in the Snowball Earth article is about 350 times today's CO2, though some scientists consider that unreasonably large.

Melting does run away once it starts, but only after the push passes the upper tipping point. Below it, a little extra warmth just settles into a slightly warmer snowball, as you saw at the brighter settings.

In the model, waiting alone changes nothing. With sunlight fixed inside the band, the snowball is a stable valley and nudges are pushed back. In the real story it was the slow build-up of volcanic gas, not time itself, that ended it.

terms.means: When a system's state depends on its history: going down and coming back up follow different paths, so the switch-back point differs from the switch-in point
The moment, as a setting changes, when a stable balance and an unstable one meet and vanish together, leaving the system nowhere to rest nearby

model.title: Sunlight kept versus heat glowed away, and where the planet drifts from any start
model.note: Teaching model: the same one-layer planet as before. It keeps ¼ × sunlight × (1 − reflectiveness) and radiates 0.61σT⁴, with the smooth ice switch of Herbert et al. (2011, Eq. 18). Reflectiveness rises from the slider's ice-free value to 0.6 for icy ground, centred on 273.15 K (narrower than the paper's 15 K width). Changed here: the drift readouts now repeat the simple settling rule ten times instead of eight. Each round moves the temperature by (heat gained − heat lost) divided by how fast glowing grows with temperature, capped at 15 K a round. This is a shortcut for finding where the planet ends up, not the paper's time evolution, and it says nothing about how many years the trip takes. The temperature slider stands for the planet's history: set it to where the planet last settled. With ice on and reflectiveness 0.3, the warm state vanishes near 97% of today's sunlight and the snowball vanishes near 111%. The paper's two-layer model found about 98% and 108%, so these are close but not its results. There are no oceans, clouds, seasons, geography or heat transport, and real snowball episodes were driven by greenhouse gases rather than by changes in the Sun. Numbers are illustrative.

series.label: Sunlight kept
series.expr: 342 * sun / 100 * (1 - albedo - (ice_on > 0.5 ? max(0.6, albedo) - albedo : 0) * logistic(0.2 * (273.15 - x)))

steps.say: Same picture as before. One curve is the sunlight the planet keeps, the other is the heat it glows away, and the planet rests where they cross. Ice is switched on.
New in this step: treat the temperature slider as the planet's memory. It shows where the planet was living just before you change the sunlight.
The drift marker shows where the planet ends up, now after ten rounds of drifting instead of eight. Next we'll turn the Sun down, then back up.

explore.prompt: Run the loop yourself. Keep ice on and leave reflectiveness alone. Before each sunlight change, move the temperature slider to where the planet last settled, because that is its history.

goals.text: Start a warm planet and find the brightest sunlight at which it still slides into a snowball (leave reflectiveness as it is).
goals.when: ice_on > 0.5 && abs(albedo - 0.3) < 0.01 && temp_now >= 280 && temp_now <= 300 && settled < 273 && sun >= 95
hints: Switch ice on and start the planet at its warm balance for today's Sun.
Lower the sunlight one notch at a time and watch whether the drift marker jumps to the cold side of the freezing line.
The warm crossing disappears just below today's sunlight. You want the first notch where the marker lands left of freezing.

goals.text: Now start the planet frozen and find the dimmest sunlight that thaws it back to warm (leave reflectiveness as it is).
hints: A frozen planet starts where it last settled, so move the temperature slider down into the snowball.
Raise the sunlight one notch at a time. At first the drift marker barely moves.
It takes sunlight well above today's. Keep going until the cold crossing near 260 K vanishes.

feedback.correct: Yes. A snowball is a stable valley across a whole band of forcing. Warming that would have kept Earth unfrozen is far less than warming that pushes a frozen Earth past the upper tipping point, which is why escape estimates call for enormous CO2 build-ups.
feedback.incorrect: The trap is assuming the climate retraces its path. It doesn't: the bright ice keeps throwing away the extra warmth, so a frozen planet only escapes when the push passes the second, higher tipping point, far beyond where it fell in.

steps.say: Today's sunlight, ice on, planet starting warm. The kept-sunlight curve crosses the glow curve on the warm side, and the planet settles near 287 K.
Dim the Sun one notch. Near 280 K the kept-sunlight curve now sits just under the glow curve, so the warm crossing is gone. The planet slides past freezing to about 250 K.
The warm valley and the hilltop next to it met and vanished together. That event is called a saddle-node bifurcation, and it is the lower tipping point.
Record the history: the planet now lives in the snowball, so slide its temperature down to where it ended. Then bring the Sun back to today's.
This is the same sunlight that held a warm planet a moment ago, yet it stays frozen near 251 K. Its bright ice throws the sunlight away.
Brighten past today's sunlight. Even 10% more leaves a snowball near 260 K, still left of the freezing line.
One more notch, and the cold crossing finally vanishes in a second saddle-node bifurcation. The planet races up to about 297 K. It thawed far above where it froze.

Now return to today's Sun with the planet warm: it stays near 287 K. At the same 100%, it sat at 251 K a moment ago. Which climate you get depends on the planet's past. That memory is called hysteresis.

understand.explanation: You just watched a climate remember its past. With ice forming, the warm valley and the snowball valley both exist across a band of sunlight. Dim the Sun below the bottom of that band and the warm valley vanishes, so the planet freezes. Bringing the Sun back does nothing until it passes the top of the band, where the snowball valley vanishes too. Herbert, Paillard and Dubrulle found this loop in their two-layer energy balance model: three balances coexist for roughly 0.98 to 1.08 times today's sunlight, only the snowball survives below that band, and only the ice-free state survives above it. They trace this hysteresis to two back-to-back saddle-node bifurcations; our simpler model puts the edges near 97% and 111%. On the real Earth the Sun did not swing like this. Greenhouse gases play the same role, and escaping a snowball is estimated to have needed a huge build-up of volcanic CO2, a figure some scientists consider unreasonably large. These idealised models have no oceans, clouds or continents, so they show the shape of the loop, not exact thresholds for Earth.
understand.quote: Thus the hysteresis curve obtained for the temperature stems from the bifurcation structure of the dynamical system as two back-to-back saddle-node bifurcations.

check.task: Keep reflectiveness as it is and ice on. Put the model in a state where the planet gets more sunlight than today, yet it still settles as a snowball, below freezing.
check.hint: Brighter sunlight alone won't do it from a warm start. Think about where the planet has to be living already.
check.misconception: Once sunlight is brighter than it was when the planet froze, the ice must melt back. In fact the snowball stays stable all the way up to the second, higher tipping point.

connect.caption: The teaching model's balance rule, not the paper's two-layer equations: sunlight kept (left) equals heat glowed away (right). S is the sunlight slider, α the ice-free reflectiveness, Δα_{ice} the extra brightness of ice (switched on below freezing by a smooth step like the paper's Eq. 18) and T where the planet drifts. Since the ice term depends on T, one S can balance at two stable temperatures, and the start decides which.

concepts.recap: A frozen planet stays frozen as sunlight recovers and only thaws past a second, higher tipping point, so its climate depends on its history.

sources.title: Earth Syst. Dynam., 2, 13–23, 2011
sources.authors: Corentin Herbert, Didier Paillard, B. Dubrulle

sources.title: The dependence of the ice-albedo feedback on atmospheric properties
sources.authors: Philip von Paris, Franck Selsis, D. Kitzmann et al.
